To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
parenteral nutrition-associated cholestasis is associated with the administration of high doses (2-4 g/kg/d) of intravenous lipid emulsions containing high amounts of phytosterol (0.5 g/100 g lipid).
phytosterols, a component of lipid emulsions, may contribute to parenteral nutrition-associated cholestasis and liver injury.
phytosterols, which are found in lipid emulsions for parenteral nutrition, are not fully metabolised and may contribute to liver disease in patients receiving parenteral nutrition.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the mechanisms of lipid/phyto-sterol toxicity in the hepatobiliary tract and the potential role of phytosterol toxicity in the development of cholestasis and parenteral nutrition associated cholestasis.

the role of phytosterol toxicity in liver injury and the potential role of reducing phytosterol levels in parenteral lipid emulsions in preventing and/or treating liver disease in patients receiving parenteral nutrition.
the role of phytosterol metabolism in the development of liver disease in patients who are receiving long-term parenteral nutrition.

phytosterol content of intravenous lipid emulsions may contribute to the pathogenesis and progression of parenteral nutrition associated cholestasis.
phytosterols are a contributing factor to parenteral nutrition-associated cholestasis.
parenteral nutrition-associated cholestasis is caused by the combination of high doses of lipid and phytosterol.

phytosterols are associated with the pathophysiology of liver injury and cholestasis in patients receiving parenteral nutrition.
parenteral lipid emulsion with low phytosterol content is recommended in patients with parenteral nutrition-associated cholestasis.
phytosterols should be considered as a potential contributing factor to parenteral nutrition associated hepatic disease.

the use of lipid emulsions high in phytosterois should be avoided for patients at high risk of developing parenteral nutrition associated cholestasis.
